newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Access predicts 1998 Australia monetary spike.
newsitem.headline: Access predicts 1998 Australia monetary spike.

text.p: Forecasters Access Economics on Wednesday said a strengthening Australian economy would force a 250-basis-point monetary tightening over the coming 18 months, sharply more than implied by futures contracts.
The Australian dollar would also rise in that time, Access said in its monthly Economics Monitor briefing.

"We expect 90-day bank bill rates to rise during 1997/98 to over eight percent and bond yields to rise to nearly nine percent in mid-1998 as both wages growth and inflation pick up on the back of stronger economic growth," the consultancy said.
"The combination of solid growth and rising domestic interest rates pushes the A$ up to US$0.8300 by mid-1998."
The Australian dollar was trading at US$0.7750 on Wednesday.
Access saw bank bill yields at 8.4 percent in June 1998, compared with the current 5.8 percent rate.
The Reserve Bank of Australia conducts monetary policy by manipulating the interbank overnight cash rate. Short bill rates follow cash more or less automatically.
The cash rate is currently 6.0 percent, having been lowered by 50 basis points on three occasions since July 1996.
Bank bill futures anticipate a further 50-point easing in the next few months and then a gradual tightening by mid 1998 to 6.8 percent, a yield 160 points lower than the Access forecast.
The tightening would begin in late 1997, Access said, deriving the forecast from its well known model of the Australian economy.
The model predicted 6.1 bank bills in June 1997, implying little change to monetary policy between now and then.
But the model predicted the Australian dollar would rise to US$0.8170 by June.
Despite the forecast for a substantial monetary tightening, Access expects easier inflationary pressure over the coming year than does the Australian government.
Access expects core inflation to run at 2.3 percent year-average in 1996/97 ending June 30, compared with the 2.75 percent forecast that the government published last August.
Wages growth, a key determinant of monetary policy, should be 4.4 percent in 1996/97 (compared with the government forecast of 5.0 percent) and 3.5 in 1997/98 (4.5 percent).
The government is expected to revise its forecasts this month.
